answer: I'd like to talk about a failure that I am actually quite grateful for now. A failure that ultimately taught me a great deal was when I performed poorly in an important exam early in my studies. It was a financial accounting exam in the first year of my BBA, and I came very close to failing it. I had been [[overconfident]] and had not prepared nearly as thoroughly as I should have. I had done well at college, so I assumed university would be just as easy, and I spent far too much time with friends. My classmates were surprised, because I had always seemed so relaxed about studying. When the results came out, I was genuinely [[crestfallen]], and it was a humbling experience. I remember phoning my father and struggling to tell him. At first I felt quite [[demoralised]], but after some reflection I realised the failure was entirely my own doing. Rather than dwelling on it, I decided to treat it as a [[wake-up call]]. I completely changed my study habits, becoming far more [[disciplined]] and organised, and I started reviewing my notes every evening instead of cramming at the last minute. The next time around, my results improved dramatically, which proved the lesson had sunk in. Honestly, that early failure was one of the most [[instructive]] experiences of my life. It taught me that setbacks are not the end of the world but valuable opportunities to grow. I now genuinely believe that how you respond to failure matters far more than the failure itself.

followUps.q: How did your father react when you told him?
followUps.answer: Much more calmly than I expected. He told me that his business had failed more than once in the early years, and that what matters is getting back up. That conversation really helped.

followUps.q: Do you think failure is important for young people?
followUps.answer: Yes, in small doses. Failing early, when the stakes are low, teaches you humility and resilience. People who never fail can struggle badly when something finally goes wrong later in life.

note: Specified a first-year BBA accounting exam and the cause; plain 'disappointed' replaced by 'crestfallen'; added 'overconfident' and 'wake-up call' (6 marks).
